title: King Ladder??
reviewNotes: Three branches, 39 exact positions from the complete seven-piece board. Full selected king ladder alternates temporary bishop interference with discovered checks, bringing the king from f7 to c2 without stalemate. Bf8 reorganizes the bishops to remove a3; selected continuations end in independently completed Bxb2 mate. The independent Ke8 comparison is actual stalemate.
transcript: Sometimes the most brilliant [music] plans can come from the simplest positions. White seems to be completely lost. It only has two bishops left and black [music] is about to promote a pawn to a new queen, but white has a brilliant plan that is going to allow him not only to save the position, but to win the game. We start with bishop to G6, the only check available in the position. Now black has two options to either give up the knight for no reason or the other option is to simply go to the corner and from here the only winning move for white is the incredible king to F7. Now no matter what black does, we are going to get the same exact setup. If the knight tries to attack the bishop, we are going to give a check, force the knight back, and then play the very precise bishop to G7. If black had played A3, we would have played bishop to H6 and then bishop to G7. But now we can notice that there is a slight problem. The bishops are completely paralyzing the black position, which means that if we are not careful and play a random move, the king cannot come out, the knight cannot move, and the pawns are paralyzed. So this would be a draw by stalemate. But that is exactly why we played king to F7 and bishop to G7 because we wanted to be able to play king to F6. The king steps in front of the bishop and it allows the black knight to move avoiding the stalemate. [music] And some of you might think, "Well, so what? The knight moves and after we move the king, it's just going to come back and we have the same problem." But the position has changed. The king has stepped [music] it to walk down the board and it can continue this pattern. Yes, this is a king [music] ladder. The king starts marching down the board blocking the view of the bishop again and again to allow the knight to move and prevent the stalemate. >> [music] >> And eventually, it reaches the corner and yet black believes that this is still going to be a draw because the white king is always going to block the view of one of the bishops. So black plays knight check. White follows up with king to c2 check, and the knight has to come back. Now, of course, taking the knight would not be good. The pawn would take back, and black would promote to a queen on the next [music] move. The black king is convinced that he found the right defensive setup, but a shiver goes down his spine when he sees bishop to f8. [music] And all of a sudden, it dawns on him that this is completely lost. If the knight moves here, now after the bishop [music] takes the pawn, we are threatening a checkmate in one move. The knight would want to stay guarding that square, but it has to move. And after it does, this is going to be a checkmate. But, black is not that naive, and he tries to play knight to c4, now defending the a3 pawn. But, luckily, white had calculated everything. And so, after king to b3 [music] and knight back to b2, now we take on a3. The knight moves again. The last nail in this beautiful coffin is bishop to c1. Black is in zugzwang. The knight has to stay covering the b2 square, but it can't. It has to move. And after it does, we're going to finally win this incredible game.
